samples.text:
These days, a lot of people post many details about their private life on social media, for example photos of their family, where they are on holiday and what they eat every day. In my opinion, this is a negative development, because it has more risks than benefits.

Of course, there are some good points. People can keep in touch with friends and relatives who live far away, and they can share happy moments like a wedding or the birth of a baby. Some people also say that sharing their problems online help them to get support from others.

However, the first big problem is privacy and safety. When people post their address, their school or the place where they are at the moment, criminals can use this informations. For example, if a family post photos from the beach, a thief can know that their house is empty. Also, pictures of children can be seen by strangers, which is dangerous.

The second problem is that sharing everything online can make people unhappy. Many users only post the best parts of their life, so other people compare themselves and feel that their own life is boring or not successful. Some people also become addicted to getting likes and comments, and they spend more time on their phone than with the real people around them. Another risk is that the things people post can stay on internet forever. A young person may share something embarrassing today, and many years later an employer can find it and decide not to give them a job.

In conclusion, although social media helps people to stay connected, I believe sharing private life publicly is negative because it is risky for safety and it can damage people's happiness and future.
samples.why: Clear negative position · relevant ideas with simple examples but limited depth · list-like linking (first, second, Finally) · adequate vocabulary · errors with uncountable nouns, agreement and articles.

samples.text:
It has become normal for people to post photographs of their homes, children, holidays and even personal struggles on social media for anyone to see. Although this trend certainly carries risks, I believe that overall it is a positive development.

The most obvious benefit is that it helps people maintain relationships. Families are now often spread across different cities or countries, and regular updates allow relatives to feel involved in each other's lives in a way that occasional phone calls cannot. A grandparent abroad, for instance, can watch a grandchild grow up through shared photos and videos.

More significantly, openness about private life can create support and reduce stigma. When people share their experiences of illness, unemployment or the challenges of parenting, others in similar situations realise they are not alone. Online communities built around such experiences offer practical advice and emotional encouragement, and public conversations about topics that were once considered taboo, such as mental health, have helped change attitudes in society.

That said, there are genuine dangers. Personal information can be misused by criminals, and posts made carelessly may harm a person's reputation or career years later. There is also a concern that constantly comparing oneself with the carefully edited lives of others can damage self-esteem. However, these problems largely depend on how people use social media, and they can be reduced if users learn to adjust their privacy settings and think carefully before posting.

In conclusion, while sharing personal details publicly requires caution, the ability to stay connected with loved ones and to find support from people with similar experiences makes this a mainly positive development in my view.
samples.why: Clear positive position throughout · ideas extended with relevant examples · risks acknowledged and answered · logical progression and varied linkers · good vocabulary (stigma, taboo, self-esteem) · largely error-free.

samples.text:
Social media has blurred the boundary between public and private life. Details that people once shared only with close friends, such as family celebrations, health scares and relationship breakdowns, are now routinely broadcast to hundreds or even thousands of followers. While this openness has some genuine merits, I believe that, taken as a whole, it is a negative development.

It would be unfair to dismiss the practice entirely. Sharing personal news allows people to sustain relationships across great distances, and candid accounts of difficult experiences can foster solidarity and help to dismantle stigma around issues that were long hidden. For some, a supportive online audience provides comfort that is not available in their immediate surroundings.

The difficulty is that most users greatly underestimate the permanence and reach of what they post. Content shared casually can be copied, archived and rediscovered long after it has lost its original context, sometimes resurfacing when its author applies for a job. Information that seems harmless in isolation, such as a child's school uniform or a holiday departure date, can, when pieced together, expose people to fraud, stalking or burglary. Children are particularly vulnerable, since parents frequently publish details of their lives before they are old enough to consent.

There is also a subtler psychological cost. When private experiences are presented to an audience, they tend to be curated for approval, and life becomes something to be performed rather than simply lived. Constant exposure to others' highlights encourages unfavourable comparison, while the pursuit of likes can make self-worth dependent on external validation.

In conclusion, although sharing personal lives online can strengthen connections and reduce isolation, the long-term risks to privacy, safety and wellbeing are, in my view, greater. It is therefore a trend that calls for far more caution than it currently receives.
samples.why: Clear negative judgement with fair concession · ideas extended with insightful, specific consequences · paragraphing and cohesion managed skilfully · wide, precise vocabulary (curated, external validation) · varied, error-free structures.
